raw_response:
I’m farming only 5 mu, so I can’t gamble too much. What I usually think first is whether the crop can come out steady and whether I still have enough cash left at home if something goes wrong. On my land, wheat-maize is the familiar way, and with only middle school education I still listen to what the extension guy says, but I don’t follow it exactly. I look at what worked on my own field and what the better farmers nearby are doing. Last few years, if wheat gets enough base fertilizer and one topdress, plus water at the key stages, it does alright. Maize has to go in fast right after wheat, otherwise you lose time and yield. Because some family members work off-farm, I can’t depend on a lot of hand labor, so I keep the plan simple: normal wheat, normal maize, not too much experimenting, fertilizer split into a couple of times, and irrigation only at important stages because pumping water costs money.

For wheat, I’ll stay with a local improved variety and sow in early to mid October, around the usual village timing. I’ll put most of the phosphorus and potassium and part of the nitrogen before sowing, then topdress once around jointing. If the year turns dry, I’ll irrigate about three times: once before winter or at overwintering if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around filling depending on rain. I won’t push fertilizer too high because 5 mu is small and every extra bag costs money, but I also don’t want the wheat to turn yellow and lose yield. After wheat harvest in June, I’ll plant maize right away, within a few days. For maize I’ll use hybrid seed, do simple rotary tillage or direct sow after clearing straw, put down base fertilizer, and topdress once around the big bell stage. Since I have well water, I can irrigate if July or August is too dry, but if rain is normal I’ll keep it to one time or even skip it. That way I protect yield without spending too much.
